title: Mental-status observation: describing forty minutes without describing a person

objectives.statement: Write a mental-status description that names the period observed and holds every observation inside it, attributing anything reported to its source and its own time frame, marking any conclusion as a conclusion, and attaching the observation it rests on.

Separate mood from affect in a described encounter, attributing mood to the person's own report and affect to what the examiner observed, and describe the affect by its range, the intensity of each change, and what the expression did as the subject changed, saying where the fit with the reported mood can and cannot be judged.
Identify shorthand in a written description that discards or distorts what was observed, state what each phrase costs a later reader, and restore the description the observation supported.

scenes.title: Two notes, one afternoon
scenes.contentHtml:
Two notes, one afternoon

Two people sat in on R.'s first appointment. It ran from 14:15 to 14:55 on a Thursday. R. is 34, works rotating night shifts in a warehouse, and had come to the clinic from a shift that finished at seven that morning. Afterwards both observers wrote up what they had seen.

Here is the first.

34yo, night shifts, poor historian. 4/12 low mood. Flat affect, poor eye contact, psychomotor retardation. Denies SI. Poorly motivated, refused water. Difficult to get a history from. Alcohol +.

Here is the second.

Seen 14:15 to 14:55, first appointment, having finished a night shift at 07:00 the same morning. Kept a work fleece on throughout and asked twice for the window to be closed. Sat leaning forward, forearms on knees. Looked at the floor for most of the interview, met my eye when asked a direct question, then looked away. Speech at ordinary volume and pace while describing the warehouse; pauses of five to ten seconds before answering about the last four months. Voice hoarse throughout, and R. said it had been like that "for a while". Face still for most of the forty minutes, with a brief smile while describing a colleague's joke about a forklift and eyes filling while talking about not having seen friends since spring. Asked how R. felt in themselves: "Flat. Like I'm watching it through glass." Gave the same four-month account twice with the same dates and added nothing to it when invited. Asked directly about not wanting to be alive: said there had been thoughts that life is not worth the effort, no plan, no intent, nothing acted on; said this evenly, without changing posture, and answered the follow-up questions. Offered water and declined. Rose from the chair slowly. Checked the clock twice near the end and said the bus was at 15:10.

Both writers were in the room for the same forty minutes.

Check
id check-what-was-lost

Before reading on, write two lists.

  1. Everything the first note tells you that you could not work out from the second.
  2. Everything the second note tells you that the first has discarded.

Keep both. The rest of this lesson is an argument about the second list.

The first list has one honest entry. "Alcohol +" appears in the first note and nowhere in the second, and it is a real piece of information, badly stored. Everything else in the first note is a conclusion about R. that the observations in the second note would have had to earn.

The second list runs to a page. That asymmetry is the whole subject here.

The examination has a clock on it

A mental-status examination describes how a person looked, spoke, moved, and responded during the evaluation itself. It covers a stretch of time with a beginning and an end. The history covers R.'s four months; the examination covers the forty minutes.

That reads like a filing convention until you look at what the second note put in its opening sentence. R. had been awake since the previous evening. Slow to answer, still face, low energy describes a person eight hours off a night shift about as well as it describes anything psychiatric, and no amount of care in the wording will separate those two readings on its own. A reader who has the shift time can hold both open. A reader who does not will hand the whole picture to R.

So every sentence that reports an observation has to survive the addition of during those forty minutes.

  • "R.'s face was still for most of those forty minutes" survives, and says something a reader can use.
  • "R. is flat" does not survive, because it was never a statement about the forty minutes in the first place.

Call it the clock test. It costs a second per sentence, and it catches most of what goes wrong here. An observation that fails it has stopped describing a period and started describing a person.

The examination is not made only of observations, and the clock test is not a rule against writing anything else down. R.'s account of how the last four months have felt belongs in the record, and it obviously does not describe the forty minutes. What it needs is the other half of the pair: a stated source and a stated period, so a later reader can see that it is R.'s report about four months and not the examiner's observation of an afternoon. Scene three calls that the source test, and the two work together. An observation is anchored to the encounter. A report is anchored to whoever gave it and to whatever stretch of time they were describing. What goes wrong is a sentence that carries the content of the second while borrowing the authority of the first.

What you are bringing with you

Description, inference, and interpretation (PSY-101.02) separated three things a listener does with an encounter: report what was said and seen, draw a conclusion from it, and give that conclusion a meaning. This lesson does not rebuild the separation. It applies the separation to one written document, where losing it costs a later reader the ability to tell which of the three they are holding.

Setting, role, and consent (PSY-130.01) settled the room, the purpose of the appointment, what R. agreed to, and what R. was told about the record. Take all of that as done.

Where this goes

By the end of the lesson you should be able to:

  • write a mental-status description that names the period observed and holds every sentence inside it;
  • keep mood and affect apart, attributing one to what R. reported and the other to what was seen, and describe affect by its range, its intensity, and its fit with what R. said;
  • find the shorthand in a written description that has discarded information, and put back what the observation supported.
Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R., both notes, and every detail in them were invented for this course. Nothing here assesses a real person, and no part of this lesson authorises you to examine, describe, or diagnose anyone.

Source Note
claims claim-mse-describes-observation-periodsources source-statpearls-mse

A clinical reference chapter on the mental-status examination supports the statement that the examination sets out the person's state during the evaluation itself, which is why the period observed belongs in the document. That chapter describes the examination as it is conventionally taught and written; it is not a study of how well any particular description works. R., the appointment, and both notes are inventions of this course.

scenes.title: Two words the room uses interchangeably
scenes.contentHtml:
Two words the room uses interchangeably

R. said "flat". The first note says "flat affect". The same word is in both, and it changed jobs on the way across.

In ordinary speech, mood and affect are near-synonyms and nobody is harmed by the overlap. In a psychiatric description they name two different things with two different sources, and a note that lets one slide into the other reports something nobody saw.

Check
id check-sort-mood-affect

Four items from the appointment. Sort each one into what R. reported or what the observers saw. Write your answers down before reading on.

  1. "Flat. Like I'm watching it through glass."
  2. A brief smile while describing the forklift joke.
  3. Four months of low mood, by R.'s account.
  4. Eyes filling while talking about friends.

Items 1 and 3 came from R. Items 2 and 4 came from the room. That sorting is the distinction, and the two words mark it.

Definition
id definition-mood-and-affectlabel Mood and affect

Mood is the person's own account of their sustained emotional state. It comes from what they tell you, it covers whatever period they are describing, and it is written in their words wherever they have given you words.

Affect is the emotional expression the examiner observed during the encounter: the face, the voice, the posture, and how those moved as the conversation moved. It covers the period you were in the room.

One is reported. The other is watched. Neither substitutes for the other, and each is attributed separately: an observed expression written into the mood line, or a reported state written into the affect line, loses the distinction the record depends on.

Separate is not the same as unrelated. Holding the two side by side is exactly what congruence means, and a gap between them is worth noticing and worth asking about. What the gap does not do is settle anything on its own, and it is never a licence to overwrite one line with the other.

Describing an affect instead of grading one

Affect has parts, and naming them keeps a description from collapsing into a single adjective.

  • Range is how much of the available expression appeared. The conventional words run from flat, through blunted and restricted, up to full and broad.
  • Intensity is how strong a change was when it came.
  • Reactivity is whether the expression moved with what was being discussed. Reference chapters do not list this as a separate descriptor the way they list the others; what they carry instead is labile, which marks expression that shifts markedly and quickly. Record what you saw move and when, rather than reaching for a one-word grade.
  • Congruence is whether what appeared fits the mood the person has reported and the subject they are on.

Now R., in those terms.

R.'s mood, as R. gave it: "Flat. Like I'm watching it through glass." That goes into the note inside quotation marks. A paraphrase would replace R.'s account of R.'s state with the observer's, which is the one substitution this line exists to prevent.

R.'s affect across the forty minutes: the face was still for most of the appointment; it changed twice, once towards a smile and once towards tears; both changes tracked what was being talked about; neither was strong or long. Written out: narrow range, low intensity, reactive to content, congruent with the mood R. described.

Where the first note went wrong

"Flat affect" fails twice over.

Flat, used technically, names expression that barely moves at all. This face moved twice in forty minutes, and both times it moved in the direction the conversation was going. On the standard vocabulary the word is simply the wrong one, and narrow range with preserved reactivity is the description that fits.

The second failure is the interesting one. The word arrived in the affect line because R. used it about mood. One person's word for how they feel inside became the examiner's word for what their face did, and the note now carries a single observation twice while appearing to carry two.

That migration runs in both directions and is worth watching for. An observer who has watched a still face for half an hour and writes "mood: flat" has done the same thing backwards, replacing what R. said with what the observer saw.

Why a description outlives a label

Five senior psychiatrists once rated affect from the same recorded interviews, each seven to ten minutes long, with 25 inpatients. Their mean agreement was 54% on the quality of the affect, 43% on its range, and 25% on a finer subtype. That was one small pilot at one hospital with one patient group and very short interviews, so the figures themselves belong to that study and travel nowhere.

The direction travels. The further a term sits from what was in the room, the less of it survives the trip to the next reader. Blunted has to be reconstructed by whoever reads it, and reconstruction is where the agreement went. "Two expression changes in forty minutes, both fitting the content" arrives intact, and anyone can apply their own word to it afterwards.

This is the argument for describing rather than grading, and it is an argument about information, not about manners. The manners argument comes later and turns out to be about information too.

Source Note
claims claim-mood-is-reported-affect-is-observed, claim-affect-descriptors, claim-affect-ratings-vary-between-clinicianssources source-statpearls-mse, source-barzilay-affect-rating

A clinical reference chapter on the mental-status examination supports the split between mood as the person's own reported state and affect as the examiner's reading of observed expression, and it supplies the conventional descriptors including range and congruence. The agreement figures come from a single pilot study of five raters, 25 male inpatients with schizophrenia, and interviews of seven to ten minutes; the authors themselves name the small sample and the narrow patient group as limits. Take the figures as evidence that these judgements vary, and not as an estimate of how much they vary anywhere else. R.'s words and expressions are invented for this course.

scenes.title: Writing three lines from a page of observation
scenes.contentHtml:
Writing three lines from a page of observation

The second note in the first scene is a running account of the appointment. A mental-status description is the organised version of that account, written in lines that a later reader can find. This scene builds three of those lines out loud, so that the decisions are visible while they are being made.

Nothing new is added. Everything below comes from the same forty minutes.

Worked Example
id worked-example-three-lines

Task. From the observations of R.'s appointment, write the appearance-and-behaviour line, the speech line, and the mood-and-affect line. Show every decision that could have gone the other way.

What you have. The observation log, in the order things happened.

Time What happened
14:15 Collected from the waiting area, having arrived about ten minutes early
Throughout Work fleece kept on; asked twice for the window to be closed
Throughout Sat leaning forward, forearms on knees; floor for most of the interview; met the examiner's eye on direct questions, then looked away
Throughout Voice hoarse; R. said it had been like that "for a while"
14:20 onward Ordinary volume and pace about the warehouse; five to ten second pauses before answering about the last four months
14:26 Brief smile while describing a colleague's forklift joke
14:31 Asked how R. felt in themselves: "Flat. Like I'm watching it through glass."
14:38 Eyes filled while talking about not having seen friends since spring
14:44 The four-month account repeated, same dates, nothing added when invited
14:50 Water offered and declined
14:53 Rose from the chair slowly; checked the clock twice; said the bus was at 15:10

What you do not have. Why R. moved slowly. Whether R. looks at the floor in every conversation or only in this one. What R.'s face does on a day off. Whether the hoarseness is old. None of that was in the room, and none of it can appear in a document about the room.

Principle selected. Two tests, applied to each sentence in turn. The clock test asks whether the sentence still holds when you add during those forty minutes. The source test asks whether a reader who was not present could say what happened from your sentence alone. A conclusion may go in when it earns its place, on the condition that it is written as a conclusion and carries what it rests on.

Plan. Draft each line from the log only. Run both tests on every sentence. Repair, then read the three lines as a stranger would.

Execution.

Appearance and behaviour. "Attended alone, arriving about ten minutes early, in work clothing kept on throughout the appointment, and asked twice for the window to be closed. Sat leaning forward with forearms on knees. Looked at the floor for most of the appointment and met my eye when asked a direct question. Rose slowly from the chair at the end."

Three decisions are buried in that. Work clothing kept on passes the source test; dressed inappropriately for the weather would not, because it grades R. against a standard the reader cannot see. Looked at the floor for most of the appointment and met my eye on direct questions is longer than "poor eye contact" and carries the pattern, which is the part a second reader can compare against next time. Rose slowly from the chair stays a movement; whether the slowness belongs to a mood, to a night shift, or to something in R.'s body is a question this line has no business settling.

Speech. "Ordinary volume and rate while describing work. Pauses of five to ten seconds before answering questions about the last four months. Voice hoarse throughout; R. reports it has been hoarse for some time."

The interesting decision is the contrast. Writing only "slow, long pauses" would have been true of part of the appointment and would have hidden the fact that the slowing arrived with a topic. The hoarseness sits in the speech line because that is where a later reader will look for it, and it is attributed to R.'s report where R. supplied it.

Mood and affect. "Mood, in R.'s words: 'Flat. Like I'm watching it through glass.' Affect: narrow range, low intensity; two changes in forty minutes, a brief smile and eyes filling, both congruent with what was being discussed and with the mood described."

R.'s sentence goes in whole. Two changes in forty minutes is a count, so a reader three weeks from now can compare a count with a count. Congruent with what was being discussed is a judgement, and it is written as one, with the two events attached so the reader can disagree.

Assumptions and limits. All three lines assume the observer's own attention was steady, which nobody checks. The affect line assumes the standard vocabulary means the same to the reader, which the last scene showed is only partly so, and that is why the count and the two events travel with it. Nothing in the three lines establishes that any of this is stable, characteristic of R., or present outside the appointment.

Independent check. Give the three lines to someone who was not there and ask them to say what happened in the room. If they can describe the fleece, the pauses, the two expression changes, and the bus, the lines are doing their work. If they come back with an impression and no events, something was compressed away, and the compressed part is exactly what the next appointment would have been compared against.

Interpretation. Together the three lines support a small set of statements: that R. was cold and stayed dressed for it, that slowing appeared with one subject and not others, that expression was narrow and still moved, and that R. gave a consistent, thin account. They support nothing about why. Why belongs to the history, to a physical examination, to tests, and to lessons after this one.

Self-explanation. One decision in the three lines does more work than the rest. Find it, and say what a reader loses if it goes the other way.

The decision worth naming is the one in the speech line: recording that the pauses arrived with a topic. Everything else in the three lines describes a state. That one sentence describes a pattern, and a pattern is the only thing here that a later observation can confirm or contradict. Drop it, and R. becomes a person who is slow. Keep it, and R. becomes a person who was slow about one thing on one afternoon, which is a claim somebody can go and check.

Source Note
claims claim-mse-describes-observation-period, claim-mood-is-reported-affect-is-observed, claim-affect-descriptorssources source-statpearls-mse, source-barzilay-affect-rating

The line structure, the treatment of mood as reported and affect as observed, and the descriptive vocabulary of range and congruence come from a clinical reference chapter on the mental-status examination. The pilot study of affect ratings is the reason the affect line here carries a count and two named events alongside the descriptive words. Services and record systems organise these lines differently and use different headings; what does not vary is that the document reports the evaluation period. R.'s appointment and the whole observation log were written for this lesson.

scenes.title: What "poor historian" costs
scenes.contentHtml:
What "poor historian" costs

Every clinical document is compressed. "4/12 low mood" is compression, and it is fine: four months of low mood is what it says, and a reader can unpack it exactly. "Poor historian" is a different operation. It cannot be unpacked, because the observation it replaced is no longer in the building.

The distinction is worth stating once, plainly. Compression keeps the information and shortens the writing. Shorthand of the second kind shortens the writing by throwing information away, and usually replaces it with a judgement about the person. This scene works through the first note phrase by phrase and puts back what the room supported.

Misconception
id misconception-shorthand-is-decompressible

The wrong model, stated fairly. Clinical shorthand is a professional compression code. An experienced reader decompresses "flat affect, poor historian, poorly motivated" back into roughly the right picture, so writing it out longhand is a courtesy to junior readers and costs time that busy services do not have.

Commit first. Cover the observation log from the last scene. Read this line: flat affect, poor eye contact, poorly motivated. Write down what you think the room looked like.

What the model cannot explain. Compare your reconstruction with the log. The two expression changes are almost certainly missing, because "flat" excludes them. The direct-question pattern in the eye contact is missing, because "poor" is a grade and grades have no shape. The bus at 15:10 is missing, and without it "poorly motivated" has nothing behind it at all. The code did not decompress, because there was nothing left inside it to decompress. Add to that the agreement figures from earlier in the lesson: experienced psychiatrists watching the same interview agreed on the range of affect under half the time. A code that senior readers encode differently cannot be decoded reliably by anyone.

The better model. A phrase in a mental-status description earns its place when a reader who was not present can say what happened from it. Descriptive words are welcome next to the events they summarise, where they act as a heading. Alone, they are the only copy, and they are a lossy one.

Recheck in a new case. A colleague writes: agitated, uncooperative with examination. Say what you now know about the appointment. You know that somebody formed two impressions and you know nothing about the room. Then write the two or three sentences that would have made those impressions checkable, and notice that they are not much longer.

The first note, line by line

Each row takes one phrase from the first note, sets the room beside it, and names what the phrase costs the reader who inherits it.

Wrote What was in the room What the phrase costs
poor historian Gave the same four-month account twice with the same dates; added nothing when invited to expand A consistent, thin account is evidence about the account. "Poor historian" converts it into a defect in R. and deletes the consistency, which is the useful half
flat affect Face still for most of forty minutes; two changes, both tracking the conversation Contradicts the observation on the standard vocabulary, and hides that expression was reactive when it came
poor eye contact Floor for most of the interview; met the examiner's eye on direct questions The pattern. A grade with no shape cannot be compared with anything at the next appointment
psychomotor retardation Rose slowly; five to ten second pauses before four-month questions; ordinary pace on other topics; hoarse voice That the slowing was topic-bound, and that it sat in the same room as a hoarse voice and a request to close the window
denies SI Asked directly; described thoughts that life is not worth the effort, no plan, no intent, nothing acted on; said evenly; answered the follow-up questions What R. actually said, how R. said it, the period asked about, and the fact that R. answered the follow-ups. The phrase records a negation and discards everything that made it checkable
refused water Water was offered and declined Water was offered and declined. Refused is not wrong, but declined is the plainer word and does not invite a reader to picture resistance
poorly motivated Checked the clock twice near the end; said the bus was at 15:10 A bus
difficult to get a history from Answered every question asked; elaborated little Whether the difficulty was in R., in the questions, or in the forty minutes available
Alcohol + Most evenings, more over the last two months, by R.'s account to help with sleep Amount, direction of change, and R.'s own reason, all three of which a later reader will need

Three of these rows are worth a second look.

Psychomotor retardation is not rude and it is not lazy. It is a real technical term, used correctly by many people, and it still fails the source test. It names a slowing of movement and thought as a feature of the mental state, which is a conclusion, and it absorbs the hoarseness and the cold into a psychiatric account before anyone has looked anywhere else. The last scene of this lesson returns to exactly that.

Denies SI is the phrase most likely to survive review, because everybody writes it. In clinical use it is a conventional way of recording that something was asked about and reported absent, and the reference chapter this lesson cites writes it exactly that way. The problem is not that the word is false. The problem is that it is a container with almost nothing in it. It does not say what was asked, in what words, over what period, or what R. said back.

R. was asked directly and described thoughts that life is not worth the effort, with no plan, no intent, and nothing acted on, answered evenly, and answered the follow-up questions too. Denies SI records none of that. A clinician reading the two versions a week apart is not reading the same clinical picture, and only one of them can be checked.

There is a second cost, smaller and worth knowing. Outside the ward the word still carries its ordinary sense of disputing a charge, and R. is among the people who can now read this record. A phrase whose technical sense has worn smooth for you has not worn smooth for them.

Refused water has the same shape. Water was offered and declined, and refused is not a wrong description of that. But declined is the plainer word for what happened, and refused invites the reader to picture a resistance that nobody in the room saw.

This is measurable, and it has been measured

The case for writing the second note is usually made as a matter of respect. It is also a matter of what happens next.

Four hundred and thirteen medical students and residents were randomly given one of two chart notes about the same hypothetical patient, a young man with sickle cell disease in a pain crisis. The clinical information in the two notes was identical. One was written neutrally; the other cast doubt on the patient's pain, carried unnecessary markers of lower socioeconomic status, and implied that he had been uncooperative. Readers of the stigmatising note scored the patient lower on a validated attitude scale, and the residents among them also chose less intensive pain management. The point estimates are not quoted here: the article carries a published correction whose text is not reachable through this project's permitted routes, and the figures on the article of record cannot be confirmed as the corrected ones. The direction and the fact of both differences are what the study supports, and they are what this scene needs. Nothing about the patient differed. Only the previous clinician's sentences did.

A second study read 600 outpatient notes written by 138 physicians and sorted the ways negative feeling actually shows up in a record. Five recurred: questioning the patient's credibility with words such as claims and insists or with quotation marks placed around their account, disapproving of their reasoning or self-care, quoting their speech in a way that marks them out, portraying them as difficult, and emphasising the writer's own authority over them. Look back at the first note. In twenty-eight words it questions credibility with denies, disapproves with poor historian and poorly motivated, and marks R. as difficult twice over, which is three of the five. The writer would almost certainly say they were being efficient.

A third study counted stigmatising descriptors across 48,651 hospital admission notes at one centre in a single year. Two and a half per cent carried at least one term from the study's restricted descriptor lists. After adjustment, the share was 0.67 percentage points higher in notes about Black patients than in notes about White patients, with a confidence interval running from 0.15 to 1.18. The habit is uncommon, and it is not evenly distributed.

Put the three together. The wording of a note changes what the next clinician thinks and does, negative wording has recognisable recurring forms, and it lands more often on some patients than others. Avoiding dehumanising shorthand is a documentation skill with measurable consequences, and it belongs in the same part of your training as taking a blood pressure properly.

Source Note

The technical meanings of flat and of a reactive, congruent affect come from a clinical reference chapter on the mental-status examination. The agreement figures behind the argument that a descriptive word decodes unreliably come from a single small pilot, five raters and 25 male inpatients with schizophrenia, and belong to that study rather than to psychiatry in general. The first note and the room it describes were written for this lesson.

Source Note

The randomised vignette study supplies the attitude and pain-management figures; it used one condition, one academic centre, and trainees rather than established clinicians, so it establishes that note wording transfers to the next reader and not how large that effect is elsewhere. The qualitative study of 600 notes supplies the five recurring forms of negative expression, drawn from one outpatient internal-medicine setting. The prevalence and disparity figures come from admission notes at one urban academic centre in 2018 and rest on a word list, so they count the descriptors that list contains and miss anything phrased differently. None of the three studies was conducted in psychiatry, and applying them to a psychiatric record is this lesson's inference, made because the mechanism they describe is the record itself.

scenes.title: Three passes at the same forty minutes
scenes.contentHtml:
Three passes at the same forty minutes

Three tasks, with less help each time. Attempt each one in writing before reading the response underneath it. Writing the sentence out is the point; recognising a good sentence when you see one is a weaker skill and it is not the one being built here.

First pass, with the pattern in front of you

Check
id check-practice-supported

The first note says: "Poorly motivated, refused water."

The log holds three relevant entries: water was offered and declined at 14:50; R. checked the clock twice at 14:53; R. said the bus was at 15:10.

Do three things.

  1. Name every claim the note makes that the log does not support.
  2. Write the replacement sentence for the description.
  3. Say which line of the description your sentence belongs on.

Use the two tests from the worked example: add during those forty minutes, then ask whether a reader who was not present could say what happened.

The note makes two unsupported claims and one distortion. Poorly motivated attributes a disposition to R. from an event that has an ordinary explanation sitting next to it in the log. Refused reports resistance to an offer that was simply declined. The distortion is the pairing itself: putting the two phrases in one sentence invites the reader to treat the declined water as evidence for the motivation.

A replacement: "Declined water when offered. Checked the clock twice in the last few minutes and said their bus was at 15:10." It belongs on the appearance-and-behaviour line, and it is one word longer than what it replaces.

If you wrote something like "appeared eager to leave", run the clock test again. It survives the test, which is why it is tempting, and it still fails the source test: a reader cannot get from eager to leave back to a bus.

Second pass, with the sentences supplied

Check
id check-practice-faded

A third person also sat in and wrote this paragraph.

R. presented as a guarded 34-year-old who was clearly reluctant to be there. Kept their work fleece on for the entire session. Was adamant that the sleep problem started in March. Gave very little away. Some psychomotor slowing was evident. Denied any thoughts of self-harm on direct questioning.

Label each of the six sentences as one of: an observation, a conclusion written as a conclusion, or a conclusion written as an observation. Then rewrite every sentence in the third category using only what the log supports, or mark it as unrecoverable if the log does not support it.

Sentence by sentence. Five of the six are conclusions written as observations, and the middle category is empty, which is the finding. Nowhere in the paragraph does the writer say that something is their reading of what they saw.

Guarded and clearly reluctant to be there is a conclusion written as an observation, and the log does not support it. R. arrived early. Rewrite it out of the note, or attach what it rests on if the writer has something the log does not record.

Kept their work fleece on for the entire session is an observation. It is also the one sentence in this paragraph that a later reader could use, and the paragraph gives it no weight at all.

Was adamant that the sleep problem started in March is a conclusion written as an observation. R. gave the same account twice with the same dates. Consistency became stubbornness on the way onto the page. This is the fourth of the five recurring forms that a study of six hundred real outpatient notes found: portraying the patient as difficult, usually through one loaded adjective. Rewrite: "Gave the same account of onset on two occasions, with the same dates."

Gave very little away is a conclusion written as an observation, and it is recoverable: "Answered the questions asked and added little when invited to expand."

Some psychomotor slowing was evident is a conclusion written as an observation, and was evident is doing the disguising. Rewrite: "Pauses of five to ten seconds before answering questions about the last four months; ordinary pace on other subjects; rose slowly from the chair."

Denied any thoughts of self-harm on direct questioning is a conclusion written as an observation and it is also wrong. R., asked directly, described thoughts that life is not worth the effort, with no plan, no intent and nothing acted on. The paragraph has converted a described experience into a denial. Anyone reading this note next month believes R. said no.

Third pass, on your own

Check
id check-practice-independent

The last two minutes of the appointment were left out of the earlier log. Here they are.

At 14:54 R. pulled the hood of the fleece up before opening the door and said "thanks for listening" at ordinary volume while looking at the floor. R. then stopped with a hand on the handle and asked whether the letter would go to their GP. Told that it would, R. said "fine" after a pause of about three seconds, and left at 14:55.

Write the sentence or two that belong in the mental-status description. Say which line each belongs on. Then name one conclusion you were tempted to write and did not, and say what it would have cost.

There is more than one defensible answer. A workable version: "At the end of the appointment, asked whether the letter would go to their GP and paused for about three seconds before accepting that it would." That belongs on the appearance-and-behaviour line, or on a line about how R. engaged with the appointment if the record has one.

The hood, the floor, and the volume all belong to lines that already exist and should not be repeated. "Thanks for listening" is a social remark at the door and carries nothing a reader can use, though it costs little to include.

The conclusion most people reach for is that R. was worried about the letter. It may well be right and it is not observable. Written plainly it becomes the observer's reading of a three-second pause, and the next reader inherits an anxiety that nobody witnessed. If it matters, write the pause and the question, then ask R. at the next appointment. The description's job is to leave the question available.

Where you go if a pass did not work

Missing the first pass usually means the clock test is doing all the work and the source test is doing none. Reread the two tests in the worked example, then redo the first pass asking only whether a reader who was not present could say what happened.

Missing the second pass usually means the disguised conclusions are hard to see, which is normal, because they are written in the grammar of observations. Take any paragraph you have written about anyone and underline every adjective that grades a person. Each one is a candidate.

Missing the third pass is the least worrying of the three. Independent writing from a raw observation is the hardest thing in the lesson, and the third pass has no single right answer. Compare yours with the version above and ask which of you a stranger could follow.

You will use all of this again. Mood phenomenology and function, later in the course, builds the mood picture out of a description like the one you have just written, and the outcome after it sets this appointment beside a second one months later. Both depend on the description having kept its events.

Source Note
claims claim-negative-attitude-categories-in-notessources source-park-record-attitudes

The five recurring forms of negative expression, including the loaded adjective that marks a patient as difficult, come from a qualitative study of 600 outpatient notes written by 138 physicians at one academic centre. That study describes what was found in that setting and does not estimate how common the forms are anywhere else, nor was it carried out in psychiatry. All three practice passes, the third observer's paragraph, and the last two minutes of the appointment were written for this lesson.

scenes.title: Eleven minutes, and a letter R. will read
scenes.contentHtml:
Eleven minutes, and a letter R. will read

Two settings that are not the forty minutes. Both are ordinary parts of a service, and both bend the method in a way worth working out before you meet them.

Eleven minutes in a waiting room

A support worker sat with R. from 14:04 to 14:15 and has been asked to add something to the record. What they have: R. arrived early and stood by the window instead of sitting; declined a chair twice, politely, then sat when the worker sat; watched the corridor door; said nothing except in reply; answered a question about the journey in a full sentence at ordinary pace. The worker asked R. nothing about how R. was.

Check
id check-transfer-eleven-minutes

Work all four before reading on.

  1. Write the two or three sentences this worker can honestly contribute.
  2. Say which of the description's lines they belong on, and which line the worker cannot write at all.
  3. State what changes about the clock test when the period is eleven minutes instead of forty.
  4. The clinician's note says the pauses arrived with one topic. Can the worker's eleven minutes confirm or contradict that? Say why.

One and two. Something close to "Seen in the waiting area 14:04 to 14:15. Stood by the window on arrival, declined a chair twice and sat when I did. Watched the corridor door. Spoke in reply to questions, at ordinary pace and in full sentences." Appearance and behaviour takes all of it, and speech takes the last clause.

The line the worker cannot write is mood. Mood is what the person tells you about their own state, and nobody asked. An observer with eleven minutes and no question has observations of expression and no report to compare them with, so a mood line from this encounter would be the worker's impression wearing R.'s voice. Writing "seemed low" here is exactly the migration the second scene was about, running from affect to mood.

Three. Nothing changes about the test and everything changes about what passes it. The eleven minutes are as real as the forty, and eleven minutes cannot support a statement about how much of anything appeared. Narrow range of expression needs enough time for a range to have had a chance to show. The worker can write what happened; the summarising words wait for someone who was there longer.

Four. The eleven minutes can neither confirm nor contradict it. R. was not asked about the four months, so the topic that produced the pauses never came up. This is the part people get wrong: a second observation only speaks to the first if it covered the same ground. Two descriptions of the same person taken at different times and on different subjects sit side by side without ever meeting.

The letter R. will read

Many services send the person a copy of the clinic letter, and R.'s service is one of them. R. will read the description you wrote in the third scene.

Check
id check-transfer-letter
  1. Go back through the three lines from the worked example and mark any sentence whose meaning changes when R. is the reader.
  2. Decide, for each one you marked, whether it should change, and say what a change would cost the clinician who reads the letter next.
  3. Write the one sentence you would add to the letter that would not have been in the notes.

The observational sentences do not change. "Looked at the floor for most of the appointment and met my eye when asked a direct question" says the same thing to R. as to a colleague, which is a fair test of whether it was ever a description.

The judgements change, and they change in a useful direction. "Congruent with what was being discussed" reads to a colleague as a technical statement and to R. as a stranger's verdict on their face. The repair is the one the worked example already applied: keep the judgement and keep the two events attached to it, so R. can read what was seen and disagree with the reading. A judgement with its evidence in view is answerable by the person it describes. A judgement alone is not.

The move to avoid is softening. "R. seemed a little subdued" reads gently and tells the next clinician nothing, and the next clinician is the person who has to notice if R. is different in October. A letter that has been made comfortable by removing its events has traded a real cost to R. later against an imagined one now.

The sentence worth adding is the one that says what the description is for: that it sets out what was seen on one afternoon, so that a later appointment has something to be compared against. R. is entitled to know that the document is a record of forty minutes and not a verdict. The randomised study in the fourth scene, where the wording of a note moved 413 trainees' attitudes towards a patient and the pain management the residents among them chose, is the reason it matters that the next reader knows it too.

Mastery check

The assessment holds four untimed, retakeable items worth twenty-four points. Attempt each before opening its reasoning. Mastery means all twenty-four: six for rewriting a shorthand description as a time-bound one, six for separating mood from affect in a supplied encounter, six for identifying what specific phrases discard, and six for an integrated rewrite of a description you have not seen. A missed criterion routes you to a different task, not to the same one again.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every task in this lesson can be answered in prose, in bullets, or in a table, whichever suits you, and you may type, dictate, or use assistive technology. No image, audio, video, upload, or clinical software is required, and nothing depends on colour, position on a page, dragging, sound, motion, or timing. The tables are read in ordinary reading order and every relationship they carry is also stated in the prose beside them. No task asks about your own health, mood, medication, or experiences, and none requires contact with a patient, a service, or a real record.

Recovery route

If the clock test keeps passing sentences that still feel wrong, the source test is the one doing the missing work. Take the sentence and ask what a stranger could reconstruct from it. Appeared distressed survives the clock and reconstructs nothing.

If mood and affect keep swapping places, go back to the sorting task at the start of the second scene and ask one question of each sentence: did this reach me through R.'s mouth or through my eyes.

If you can see that a phrase is shorthand and cannot produce the replacement, the observation is probably missing rather than hidden. That is worth knowing, and it is a reason to write during the appointment or immediately after it.

If Setting, role, and consent (PSY-130.01) is not yet familiar, some of the letter task will float, because who reads the record and what the person was told about it is settled there.

Source Note
claims claim-mse-describes-observation-period, claim-mood-is-reported-affect-is-observed, claim-record-language-changes-later-clinicianssources source-statpearls-mse, source-barzilay-affect-rating, source-goddu-record-language

A clinical reference chapter on the mental-status examination supports both the point that the examination reports a defined evaluation period and the split between reported mood and observed affect; the pilot study of affect ratings stands behind the preference for events over summary words when the observation is short. The randomised vignette study is the evidence that what one clinician writes reaches the next clinician's judgement; it was conducted with trainees in one centre and one condition, so it supports the direction and not a size. The waiting-room encounter and the letter are inventions of this lesson, and the practice of copying letters to patients varies between services and jurisdictions.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: the observations that belong to the body
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: the observations that belong to the body

Callout
id callout-wrap-up-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. is invented, and so is every observation in this lesson. Nothing here diagnoses R., proposes a test for R., or tells any reader how to interpret their own symptoms. Weighing what R.'s picture might be is the work of a later outcome in this course and is deliberately not attempted here.

Three observations from the room have been sitting in the corner of this lesson, and a handful of complaints from the history sit next to them.

From the room: the work fleece stayed on and the window was closed twice; the voice was hoarse throughout, and R. said it had been for a while; R. rose from the chair slowly. From the history, taken before the appointment: R. described feeling cold, being constipated, and being tired past what the broken sleep would explain, along with about six kilograms of weight loss over four months that R. was not trying to lose. No thyroid result is available.

The clinical question is short. Does the mental-status description leave a body question askable, or has it already answered it?

Run the lesson's own tools over the three observations

Apply the clock test. "Kept a work fleece on throughout and asked twice for the window to be closed" passes: it is a statement about the forty minutes and a reader can picture it. "Cold intolerance" is already a small conclusion, and it belongs in the note with its basis attached, because the fleece and the window are the whole of what was seen.

Apply the source test to the first note. Psychomotor retardation, flat affect, poorly motivated reconstructs nothing. Read that line as the only record of the appointment and the fleece is gone, the window is gone, the hoarse voice is gone, and the slow rise from the chair has been renamed as a feature of R.'s mental state. The line has not lost the observations by accident. It has absorbed them.

Ask which line each observation belongs on. The fleece and the window are appearance and behaviour. The hoarseness is speech. The slow rise is behaviour. None of the three is a mental-state finding on its own, and writing them on their own lines keeps them available to whoever reads the record with a different question in mind.

Now name what the absorbing costs. The United States National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases lists fatigue, trouble tolerating cold, and depression among the common symptoms of an underactive thyroid. That is a general fact about a common condition and it says nothing about R. What it does say is that a fleece kept on indoors, a request to close a window, and unexplained tiredness are the kind of observation a clinician somewhere downstream will want, and that a thyroid result would speak to. A note that has renamed them psychomotor retardation has made them invisible to that clinician, and nobody will know to look, because the record no longer says there is anything to look at.

What the description decides and what it does not

The description does not decide anything about R.'s thyroid. It does not rank explanations, it does not order a test, and it does not say whether the low mood, the sleep, the alcohol, or the body is the more likely account. Those comparisons belong to the mood differential and longitudinal course outcome later in this course, and they need the history, a physical examination, and results that do not exist yet.

What the description decides is whether that later work is possible. Four months from now, someone will read this note. If it holds the fleece, the window, the hoarseness, the slow rise, the topic-bound pauses, the two expression changes, and R.'s own sentence about watching it through glass, then every question anyone might want to ask is still on the table. If it holds flat affect, psychomotor retardation, poor historian, then the appointment has been converted into a verdict about a person, and the verdict is all anyone inherits.

That is the argument of the whole lesson in one line. A mental-status examination describes a period of observation so that other people can go on thinking. Shorthand that grades the person instead ends the thinking early, and it ends it in the record, where nobody can see that it happened.

Where this goes next

Mood phenomenology and function, later in the course, takes a description like the one built here and assembles the mood picture from it. Mood differential and longitudinal course, the outcome after it, sets this appointment beside a second one and asks what time reveals. Both are only as good as what this document kept.

Problem representation, further on, is the general form of the same skill: getting a case into terms that make the right question available before anyone answers it.

Source Note
claims claim-mse-describes-observation-period, claim-hypothyroid-symptom-overlapsources source-statpearls-mse, source-niddk-hypothyroidism

The mental-status examination reports the person's state during the evaluation itself, which is the reason a physical observation made in the room belongs in the record on its own line; that framing comes from a clinical reference chapter on the examination. The symptom list comes from a United States national institute's public health-information page on hypothyroidism, last reviewed in March 2021, and is used here only as a general fact about which everyday observations a clinician may later want. It is not applied to R., and no lesson in this course tells anyone what their own symptoms mean.

items.prompt: Rewrite this line as a mental-status description of the appointment. Name the period observed, hold every sentence inside it, and where you keep a conclusion, write it as a conclusion with the observation it rests on. Then state one thing your version can no longer be used to claim.
items.stimulus: A fictional first appointment. The person arrived twenty minutes after the scheduled start and was then seen for 25 minutes. The observation log holds: apologised for arriving late; sat down without removing a heavy coat; answered every question in one or two words; three times said "I don't know" to questions about the last month; looked past the examiner towards the door for most of the appointment; twice asked how long the appointment would take; spoke at ordinary volume with no long pauses; stood up as soon as the examiner said the appointment was ending. The note written afterwards reads in full: "Late. Guarded, evasive, minimal engagement. Clearly did not want to be here."

answer.correct: A complete response names the 25-minute appointment as the period described, converts each of the three judgements into the observations behind them or removes it as unsupported, keeps any retained judgement labelled with its basis, and states a claim the rewritten version no longer supports. A workable version: "Seen for 25 minutes, having arrived twenty minutes after the scheduled start and apologised for the delay. Kept a heavy coat on throughout. Answered every question, mostly in one or two words, and said 'I don't know' to three questions about the last month. Looked towards the door for most of the appointment. Asked twice how long the appointment would take. Speech at ordinary volume without long pauses. Stood as soon as the ending was announced." The version no longer supports any claim about whether the person wanted to be there.
answer.summary: Name the period, replace the three graded adjectives with what was observed, and say what the honest version can no longer claim.
answer.reasoning: Guarded, evasive, and minimal engagement each grade the person against a standard the reader cannot see, and clearly did not want to be here is an unlabelled conclusion drawn from a coat, a door, and two questions about time. The observations behind them are all in the log and are barely longer written out. The last part of the task matters as much as the rewrite: an honest description gives up the claim about motivation, and a learner who rewrites the line while keeping that claim has changed the wording without changing the document.
acceptableResponses: A response may keep a labelled conclusion such as 'my impression was of reluctance, based on the coat kept on, the repeated question about length, and standing at once' provided the basis is attached.
A response may drop the apology or the volume detail as non-contributing, provided the three graded adjectives are dealt with.
Different orderings and different line headings are acceptable; some services group these observations differently.
commonErrors: Rewriting the adjectives into softer adjectives, so that guarded becomes reserved and nothing observable is added.
Keeping the conclusion about not wanting to be there and attaching only the lateness to it, which the log does not support once the apology is included.
Omitting the period observed, which leaves the description a statement about the person.
Adding detail that is not in the log, such as the person's tone or what they were thinking.

items.prompt: Which mood-and-affect entry is the defensible one for this fictional appointment?
items.stimulus: Across a 50-minute appointment the person laughed twice while describing a family argument, then wept for about a minute when asked about their job, then returned to laughing at the same subject. Both changes were large and quick. Asked how they had been feeling, they said: "Honestly, pretty good. Better than in years."

options.text: Mood: labile. Affect: labile, wide swings during the appointment.

Mood, in the person's words: "Honestly, pretty good. Better than in years." Affect: broad range with rapid, large shifts over the 50 minutes, including laughter while describing a family argument and about a minute of weeping about work, each change tracking the subject under discussion. The period the reported mood covers was not established.
Mood: elevated, though the person's account is unreliable. Affect: inappropriate.
Mood: not assessed. Affect: laughed twice, wept once.

answer.summary: Mood comes from the person and goes in their words; affect is described by range, the size and speed of each change, and the events behind it. Where the reported mood's period was never established, the description says so instead of grading the fit between the two.
answer.reasoning: The first option puts one word on both lines and so records a single judgement twice while appearing to record two things; it also assigns an observed pattern to mood, which nobody observed. The third replaces the person's report with the examiner's reading and adds a credibility judgement the encounter does not support. The fourth is honest about the observations and throws away a mood the person supplied on request, and it gives no range, so a later reader cannot compare it with anything. The second keeps the report in the person's words, describes the affect by range, intensity, speed, and the events behind it, and records the mismatch as a judgement a reader can check. Congruence is deliberately not keyed here: the reported mood covers an unstated interval and each observed change tracked its own subject, so the record's job is to describe both lines accurately and leave the relationship between them open for clarification.
commonErrors: Treating an observed pattern of expression as evidence about mood, which is the migration this lesson's second scene works through.
Reading a mismatch between report and observation as licence to overwrite the report.
Recording events without any descriptive summary, which leaves nothing for a later appointment to be compared against.

items.prompt: Select every phrase below that discards or distorts what was observed, so that a later reader cannot recover it.
items.stimulus: All five phrases come from notes about fictional appointments in which the following were observed: a person answered every question and gave the same account twice; a person was offered a leaflet and said no thanks; a person's appointment ran from 09:30 to 10:05; a person said they had been drinking most evenings and more over the past two months; a person paused for around eight seconds before each question about the past year.

options.text: Pauses of around eight seconds before questions about the past year.

answer.summary: Poor historian, refused, and alcohol excess each replace an observation with a judgement; the time and the pauses keep what was seen.
answer.reasoning: Poor historian deletes the consistency of the account and relocates the problem into the person. Refused reports resistance where a leaflet was declined, and the single verb invents a conflict for the next reader to inherit. Alcohol excess drops the amount, the direction of change, and the person's own account, and adds a threshold that nobody in the room set. The appointment times are compression that a reader can unpack exactly, and the pause description carries the event, its size, and the topic it attached to, which is what a later appointment can be compared against.
commonErrors: Selecting the appointment times because they are short, which confuses compression with the loss of information.
Leaving refused unselected because it seems factual, when declined is the word for what happened.
Leaving alcohol excess unselected because the person did describe heavy drinking, when the phrase still discards the amount, the change over two months, and the reason they gave.

items.prompt: Rewrite this description so that a clinician meeting the person in three months can use it. Name the period observed, separate mood from affect and attribute each correctly, replace every phrase that has discarded an observation, and finish with one sentence naming a question your version leaves open that the original had closed.
items.stimulus: A fictional review appointment. The observation log holds: appointment ran 11:10 to 11:40; the person arrived with a friend and asked that the friend wait outside; wore a coat and scarf indoors and said the building was cold; spoke quietly throughout, at ordinary pace, and was asked twice to repeat an answer; smiled once when the examiner mispronounced their surname and did not change expression otherwise; asked how they had been feeling, said "Same as before. Numb, mostly."; said they had stopped their evening walks in January and could not say why; asked directly about thoughts of not wanting to be alive, said there had been none since the last appointment and asked whether that would be written down. The note written afterwards reads in full: "Review. Flat affect, quiet, numb. Non-compliant with exercise advice. Nil SI. Brought a friend, sent them out. Unremarkable."

answer.correct: A complete response names the 30-minute period, records mood in the person's own words ("Same as before. Numb, mostly."), describes affect separately by what was seen (one expression change in thirty minutes, at the mispronounced surname; otherwise unchanged; narrow range) and marks any congruence statement as a judgement, replaces non-compliant with the observation (stopped evening walks in January and could not say why), replaces nil SI with what was asked and answered (asked directly, reported none since the last appointment, and asked whether it would be recorded), keeps the coat and the stated cold as an observation on its own line, and removes unremarkable. The closing sentence names a question the rewrite leaves open, such as why the walks stopped, or whether the quiet speech was new, or what the person's question about the record was about.
answer.summary: Name the period, split reported mood from observed affect, restore the four discarded observations, and say which question the honest version keeps open.
answer.reasoning: The original closes four questions at once. Flat affect contradicts an observed expression change and takes the person's word numb across into the affect line. Non-compliant converts a stopped habit with an unknown reason into a failure by the person, and deletes the January date, which is the part a three-month comparison needs. Nil SI records an absence where a question was asked, answered, and followed by a question of the person's own about the record. Unremarkable is a verdict that no later reader can check. The coat and the stated cold survive in neither version unless the learner puts them back, and they are the observation most likely to matter to someone asking a different question. The final sentence is the test of whether the learner has understood the trade: an honest description gives up conclusions in exchange for keeping questions available.
acceptableResponses: Different line headings and orderings are acceptable, since services organise the examination differently.
A response may retain a summarising word such as narrow range beside the observed event, and may note that one expression change in thirty minutes is a short basis for a range.
A response may treat the person's question about the record as belonging to the consent and documentation part of the encounter instead of the examination, provided it is not deleted.
Several different open questions are acceptable in the closing sentence, provided the question is one the original note had closed.
commonErrors: Keeping flat affect because the person used the word numb, which repeats the migration between the mood and affect lines.
Replacing non-compliant with a gentler judgement such as struggling with motivation instead of with the stopped walks and the unknown reason.
Writing denies rather than recording that the person was asked and what they said.
Dropping the coat and the stated cold as irrelevant, which is the observation a later reader with a different question would most want.
Ending with a summary of the rewrite instead of naming a question the rewrite leaves open.

criteria.description: Names the period observed and holds every sentence inside it.
Replaces each of the three graded judgements with the observation behind it, or removes it as unsupported.
States a claim the rewritten version no longer supports.
Selects the entry that keeps the reported mood in the person's words and describes the affect by range, change, events, and fit.
Selects poor historian, refused written information, and alcohol excess.
Leaves the appointment times and the described pauses unselected, distinguishing compression from loss.

rubrics.title: Integrated rewrite for a later reader

criteria.description: Names the observed period and organises the description into findable lines.
Records mood in the person's words and describes affect separately from what was observed, without carrying one across into the other.
Replaces non-compliant, nil SI, and unremarkable with what was observed, and retains the coat and the stated cold.
Names one question the rewritten version leaves open that the original had closed.

claims.statement: A mental-status examination sets out how a person appeared, spoke, moved, and responded during the evaluation itself, so it reports a defined period of observation while the history carries the longer course.
claims.scope: The conventional purpose and scope of the examination as set out in a current clinical reference chapter; the sectioning, headings, and required detail vary between services and record systems.
claims.uncertainty: The reference chapter describes established practice and does not report evidence on how well any particular way of writing the examination performs.

claims.statement: In psychiatric description, mood is the person's own account of their sustained emotional state and is recorded in their words where they have supplied them, while affect is the examiner's reading of the emotional expression shown during the encounter.
claims.scope: A descriptive convention of psychiatric assessment, stated in a current clinical reference chapter and restated in the introduction of a pilot study of affect rating.
claims.uncertainty: The convention is standard in teaching and is applied inconsistently in practice; the same pilot study reports that clinicians hold differing conceptions of the two terms.

claims.statement: Affect is conventionally described by qualities including its range, which runs through terms such as flat, blunted, restricted, full, and broad, by the intensity of a change when it comes, and by whether it is congruent with the mood the person reports.
claims.scope: The descriptive vocabulary listed in a current clinical reference chapter on the mental-status examination. That chapter names range terms, illustrates intensity by contrasting minimally irritated with extremely agitated, and defines congruent and incongruent against the reported mood. It does not name reactivity as a separate dimension, so this lesson presents reactivity as an observation to record rather than as part of the conventional descriptor set, and says so where it appears.
claims.uncertainty: The vocabulary is not standardised across services or textbooks, and individual terms such as blunted and restricted are used with overlapping meanings.

claims.statement: When five senior psychiatrists rated affect from the same recorded interviews of seven to ten minutes with 25 inpatients, mean agreement between raters was 54% for the quality of the affect, 43% for its range, and 25% for a finer subtype.
claims.scope: One pilot study at a single hospital with five raters, 25 male inpatients with schizophrenia, and brief recorded interviews; the figures describe that setting only.
claims.uncertainty: The authors name the small sample, the single site, the restriction to male inpatients with schizophrenia, the absence of standardised symptom scales, and the short interviews as limits, and expect different performance where affect varies more. The figures are evidence that these judgements vary and are not an estimate of agreement in psychiatry generally.

claims.statement: In a randomised study of medical students and residents reading one of two chart notes about the same hypothetical patient, readers of the stigmatising note rated the patient less favourably on an attitude scale, and residents reading it chose less intensive pain management.
claims.scope: One randomised vignette study of trainees at a single urban academic medical centre, using one clinical condition and a hypothetical patient.
claims.uncertainty: The article carries a published correction that could not be retrieved through permitted routes, so no point estimate is asserted. One centre, hypothetical vignette, single clinical scenario.

claims.statement: A qualitative study of 600 outpatient encounter notes written by 138 physicians identified five recurring ways negative attitude appeared in the record: questioning the patient's credibility, expressing disapproval of their reasoning or self-care, stereotyping through quoted speech, portraying the patient as difficult, and emphasising the physician's authority over the patient.
claims.scope: Notes from one ambulatory internal-medicine setting at a single urban academic centre in 2017, analysed qualitatively.
claims.uncertainty: The study describes the forms found in that sample and does not estimate how common each form is in other settings or in psychiatric records.

claims.statement: Across 48,651 hospital admission notes written at one urban academic medical centre in 2018, 2.5% contained at least one term from lists of stigmatising descriptors, and after adjustment the share was 0.67 percentage points higher in notes about Black patients than in notes about White patients, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.15 to 1.18.
claims.scope: A cross-sectional count of admission notes at one centre in a single year, using condition-specific lists of descriptors.
claims.uncertainty: The measure detects only the descriptors on the lists used, so it undercounts stigmatising writing phrased in other ways, and a count of words does not establish the writer's intent or the consequence for any patient. The setting was general hospital medicine and not psychiatry.

claims.statement: Fatigue, trouble tolerating cold, and depression are among the common symptoms of hypothyroidism listed by the United States National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.
claims.scope: A public health-information page from a United States national institute, last reviewed in March 2021, describing common symptoms of an underactive thyroid in general terms.
claims.uncertainty: A symptom list establishes that these complaints are recognised features of the condition and establishes nothing about how often any one of them indicates it in a given person. The lesson uses the fact only to show why such observations must stay visible in a record, and applies it to no one.

terms.definition: The part of a psychiatric assessment that describes how a person appeared, spoke, moved, and responded during the evaluation itself. It reports a period of observation with a stated beginning and end; the history carries the longer course.

The person's own account of their sustained emotional state. It reaches the record through what they say, it covers whatever period they are describing, and it is written in their words wherever they have supplied words. In ordinary speech mood and affect are interchangeable; in a psychiatric description they are not, and this lesson keeps them apart.

The emotional expression an examiner observed during an encounter: the face, the voice, the posture, and how those moved as the conversation moved. It reaches the record through the examiner's eyes and covers only the period observed. Affect is not evidence of mood and mood is not evidence of affect.

How much of the available emotional expression appeared during the observed period. The conventional descriptive words run from flat, through blunted and restricted, up to full and broad. A range can only be described over a period long enough for expression to have had a chance to vary.

Whether the affect observed fits the mood the person has reported and the subject being discussed. Congruence is a judgement, so a description records it alongside the observed events it rests on, which lets a later reader, or the person described, disagree with the reading.

This lesson's first check on a sentence in a mental-status description: does the sentence still hold when you add the words during those forty minutes. A sentence that fails has stopped describing a period of observation and started describing a person.

This lesson's second check on a sentence in a mental-status description: could a reader who was not present say what happened in the room from this sentence alone. A sentence that fails has replaced an observation with the writer's conclusion about it.

A phrase that shortens a clinical description by discarding the observation behind it and putting a judgement about the person in its place, as poor historian, poorly motivated, and denies do. It is distinguished from ordinary compression, which shortens the writing while leaving the information recoverable.

attributionHtml:
Attribution

Lesson authorship and licence

Mental-status observation: describing forty minutes without describing a person (PSY-INT-004), version 0.1.0, was prepared for EmbeddedKnowledge under the accountable principal VSBDev (github:VSBDev). The lesson prose, the fictional case, the two notes, the observation log, the tables, the prompts, the assessment, the glossary, and the structured records are original to this pack and are offered under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence.

No image, audio, video, diagram, dataset, software, patient record, diagnostic-manual text, rating-scale item, or clinical case from a third party is included, and the pack contains no assets/ or diagrams/ directory. R., the appointment, both notes, the third observer's paragraph, the support worker, the letter, and every fictional appointment used in the assessment were invented for this course. R. is the shared teaching case of the psychiatry interviewing block and does not describe any real person.

Sources used for facts only

Six sources were consulted, and each was used only as a factual reference. No wording, sentence order, table, figure, vignette, word list, scale item, or organisational structure from any of them appears in this pack. The lesson's explanation, examples, questions, and assessment are its own.

  • source-statpearls-mse — Voss RM, Das JM, Mental Status Examination, StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK546682, chapter last updated 30 April 2024. Consulted for the purpose and scope of the examination, the separation of mood from affect, and the conventional descriptive vocabulary for affect. The chapter is displayed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, which this corpus does not accept for reuse of expression; nothing from it is reused.
  • source-barzilay-affect-rating — Barzilay R and colleagues, Front Psychiatry. 2019;10:288, CC BY 4.0. Consulted for the reported inter-rater agreement figures, the study's sample and interview length, and its stated limitations.
  • source-goddu-record-language — Goddu AP and colleagues, J Gen Intern Med. 2018;33(5):685–691. Consulted for the randomised vignette design, the sample, and the attitude and pain-management figures. The article remains under its publisher's terms.
  • source-park-record-attitudes — Park J and colleagues, JAMA Netw Open. 2021;4(7):e2117052, CC BY. Consulted for the five recurring categories of negative expression found in encounter notes.
  • source-himmelstein-stigmatizing-terms — Himmelstein G, Bates D, Zhou L, JAMA Netw Open. 2022;5(1):e2144967, CC BY. Consulted for the prevalence figure and the adjusted difference between patient groups.
  • source-niddk-hypothyroidism — National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, Hypothyroidism (Underactive Thyroid), last reviewed March 2021. Consulted for the list of common symptoms, used in the clinical wrap-up as a general fact and applied to no one.

Agent access to each source was checked on 25 July 2026 and recorded in references.json. The NCBI Bookshelf robots file was read in full for this run; it disallows /books/?term= search queries for unnamed agents and does not disallow the chapter path used. No login, paywall, rate limit, robots rule, or other technical control was bypassed for any source.

Agent assistance and provenance

An authoring agent materially researched, designed, and wrote this candidate under the accountability of VSBDev.

  • Provider: RUNTIME-STAMPED
